title: Allocation Fragmentation & KV Cache Recovery — SKU Comparison (draft)
body:
Goal:
Short: quantify how GPU memory allocation fragmentation interacts with KV-cache lifecycles and causes transient capacity loss across cloud SKUs + driver/CUDA variants.
Why: We see intermittent p99 spikes and unexpected KV evictions in production when context lengths or concurrent sessions increase; hypothesis is allocator fragmentation + driver pin/unpin overheads cause temporary unusable memory leading to spill/evict behavior and latency amplification.

High-level findings (summary):
- Large contiguous free regions reduce eviction pressure: A100-80GB and A100-40GB SKUs with our tuned pool allocator showed ~30–45% fewer KV evictions versus L40S in the same workload pattern.
- H100 shows improved long-term fragmentation compaction (less steady-state waste) but higher short-term allocator latency when many small allocations are churned (seen as 8–12% higher per-token p99 under microburst decode).
- L40S had the most volatile behavior: good sustained throughput for decoding, but frequent small-region fragmentation (our fragmentation metric F > 0.22) leading to spike in NVMe spill operations during multi-tenant mixes.
- CUDA/driver mismatch matters: CUDA 12.x + driver D525 produced noticeably fewer pin/unpin stalls vs older stacks (CUDA 11.8 + D470) on H100 in our experiments — measured as ~6–9ms reduction in allocation tail.

Experiment matrix (what we ran):
- GPUs / SKUs: AWS p4d.24xlarge (A100-40GB), GCP a2-ultragpu (A100-80GB), Azure ND H100 v4 (H100-80GB), GCP l4 (L40S-48GB equivalent).
- Models: Llama-2-13B-chat (sharded), Llama-2-70B (quantized int8, KV-heavy), MPT-30B for mid-size comparison.
- Workloads: (A) long-context chat (prompt 16k prefills, decode 4k), (B) multi-concurrent short sessions (8 sessions * 1024 tokens), (C) allocator stress pattern: repeated prefill/evict cycle to emulate many independent conversations attaching/detaching kv caches.
- Drivers/CUDA: CUDA 11.8 + driver D470, CUDA 12.1 + driver D510, CUDA 12.2 + driver D525.
- Repetition: 10 full runs per cell, each run = 30 minutes steady-state + 10-minute microburst phase.

Instrumentation and metrics captured (notes):
- Runtime probes: allocation call-count, average alloc size, free-list fragmentation (simple metric: 1 - (largest_free_block / total_free)), per-allocation latency histogram (ns), nvme-spill count (per minute), kv-cache-evict events and evict reason, p50/p95/p99 latency for first-token and per-token decode.
- OS/proc: /proc/pid/smaps like sampling (where allowed), GPUprocess memory map via nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps.
- Kernel tracing: eBPF probes around cudaMalloc/cudaFree (where possible on the host) to get driver-side latency and syscalls.
- Notes: fragmentation metric is heuristic (see method below) — not a guaranteed physical fragmentation measure but correlates well with observed evictions in our runs.

Method (repro steps):
1) Start instance with the chosen SKU and install driver/CUDA stack per test cell.
2) Launch serving runtime with ALLOCATOR=pool_v2 (tunable: pool_chunk=64MB, max_pool=80% of GPU RAM) and PROFILER=alloc_trace.
3) Run workload harness (in scripts/frag_harness.sh) that executes prefill + decode loops and records runtime metrics to /tmp/frag_out/${run_id}.json.
4) Postprocess with tools/frag_analysis.py to compute fragmentation metric and align evict events.

Commands (reference):
- start server: ./serve --model rw-llama-13b --allocator pool_v2 --pool-chunk 67108864 --max-pool-pct 80 --profiler alloc_trace --port 8080
- harness: python tools/frag_harness.py --target localhost:8080 --pattern long_context --duration 2400 --log /tmp/frag_out/run.json
- capture eBPF: sudo ./tools/run_alloc_ebpf.sh --pid ${SERVER_PID} --out /tmp/ebpf-${run}.log

Representative results (selected highlights — median over runs shown):
- Workload A (long-context prefill heavy):
  - A100-80GB (CUDA12.1/D510): per-token throughput 830 tok/s, p99 per-token latency 13.2ms, KV-evict-rate 0.4/min, fragmentation F ~ 0.09.
  - H100-80GB (CUDA12.2/D525): throughput 890 tok/s, p99 per-token latency 14.4ms (higher tail), KV-evict-rate 0.6/min, fragmentation F ~ 0.07.
  - L40S-48GB (CUDA12.1/D510): throughput 760 tok/s, p99 per-token latency 16.8ms, KV-evict-rate 1.9/min, fragmentation F ~ 0.24.
- Workload B (concurrent sessions):
  - A100-40GB (p4d) shows stable throughput until ~64 concurrent sessions; after that fragmentation and evictions escalate rapidly unless pool_chunk increased.
  - H100 shows smoother degradation but higher short-term alloc spikes caused by driver-side pin/unpin latency (visible in eBPF traces as 2–12ms stalls on cudaHostAlloc calls).

Interpretation and root causes (diagnostic notes):
- Fragmentation source: repeated creation/destruction of small KV tensors (~8–64KB ranges) results in many small free blocks that cannot be stitched by our allocator because we returned blocks to driver/OS rather than coalescing across pool boundaries. Over time these small holes increase the chance that a subsequent large prefill cannot find contiguous space and triggers eviction/spill.
- Driver behavior: newer drivers reduce some of the overhead but introduce different pin/unpin batching heuristics which reduce steady-state overhead but worsen microburst tails on H100.
- NVMe spill correlation: observed spikes in NVMe writes immediately after allocation failures; these wrote out KV pages and then reloaded them, which produced both latency spikes and increased IO cost.

Immediate mitigations we tested: (quick wins)
- Increase pool_chunk from 64MB -> 128MB: reduces fragmentation growth rate by ~18% in multi-session patterns. Tradeoff: larger chunks increase internal wasted space at low concurrency.
- Proactive pre-allocation for common prefill sizes: reserving a small bag of large free blocks ahead of heavy prefill reduced evictions by ~40% for workload A.
- Driver stack upgrade to D525 on A100 improved alloc tail by ~7% for steady-state but had mixed results on H100.

Longer-term changes to evaluate: (prioritized)
1) Coalescing allocator changes: allow cross-pool coalescing and delayed return-to-driver policy. Expected to reduce F by 0.10–0.15 in our synthetic tests.
2) Hot/Cold KV tiering: keep frequently accessed prefixes in a pinned region and allow low-cost spill for cold fragments; requires KVS hotset detector.
3) Precompact routine: background defragmentation pass during low-util windows (experimentally feasible but needs correctness review for asynchronous KV refs).
4) Fall-back policy tuning: earlier fallback to smaller-model-variant instead of NVMe spill when we detect fragmentation k-slope — reduces p99 spikes but increases model-quality regressions.

Open questions / unknowns (to investigate):
- Can we rely on driver-side compaction on future H100 firmware/driver updates, or must we own coalescing entirely? Vendors are vague.
- Eviction cost accounting: how much of total cost is NVMe IO vs CPU overhead vs additional decode time? Need finer tracing.
- Multi-tenant isolation: are small tenants causing outsized fragmentation that impacts larger tenants on shared nodes? We saw signs but need controlled isolation matrix.

Action items / next runs:
- [Aisha] Prototype a delayed free (hold-for-Xs) variant of pool_v2 and run the full matrix for 48h to capture stochastic events (SRV-1427).
- [Miguel] Add finer-grained IO timing to nvme spill path and correlate with GPU alloc traces.
- [Priya] Coordinate with hardware partners to test a pre-release H100 driver (contact: hw-partner@vendor.com).
- [Ben] Draft a change to rollout policy that prefers D525 for A100 fleet and flag H100 nodes for additional monitoring.

Appendix: reproducibility notes and gotchas
- Make sure MIG is disabled for these tests (we need full-device allocation to study contiguous region behavior).
- Use isolated tenant machines with no other background processes that perform GPU allocations (e.g., monitoring sidecars that use nvml may perturb free lists).
- On GCP, there is a known hypervisor interrupt that can delay driver pin/unpin (see linked jira). We mitigated in tests by placing instances in 'workload-optimized' host pools.

Raw artifacts location (temp): gs://redwood-inference-bench/frag/2025-09/{run_id} (note: permission-limited; use linked_artifacts PRs for approvals).

Notes-to-self (informal):
- This doc is messy — save key findings to Confluence once we lock on allocator change.
- Need to include regression test in CI that runs a 5-minute frag pattern on every allocator change.

References and related tickets:
- JIRA SRV-1427 (allocator/kv-evict investigation), GH rwrd-inference/allocator-probes#58 (ebpf probes + parser), CONFLUENCE SERVE-MEM-2025-09 (detailed spreadsheets).

End of doc.
